subjects.introduction: What did the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá suffer, and what meaning did they give to it? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They open with summaries of a life without rest, then follow the Báb’s imprisonments and martyrdom, the dungeon of Ṭihrán, the banishments to Baghdád, Constantinople and Adrianople, and the prison of ‘Akká, which Bahá’u’lláh chose to name the Most Great Prison [2]. Passages on the measure of His sorrows, including His words that the cruelties of His oppressors had turned His hair white [1], lead to the opposition faced by every Messenger, the purpose given to the sufferings and the joy found in them. The forty years of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s imprisonment, counsel to believers who share in tribulation, and prayers revealed in the prison complete the sequence. Two imported quotations follow the linked readings with their supplied wording and references.

These readings turn to the Báb. A Traveller’s Narrative records how the learned doctors agreed on His suppression, how He was held forty days in Tabríz and nine months in the castle of Máh-Kú, and how the doctors met and wrote their verdict; the same account carries Bahá’u’lláh’s words on the coming move to ‘Akká. In His own writings the Báb says that He was patient until judged without justice to imprisonment in the depths of the mountain, describes a fortress with two guards and four dogs, finds the mountain pleasant because it accords with the Beloved’s good-pleasure, and thanks God for turning the prison into a garden of Paradise. Elsewhere He asks what greater honour there could be than martyrdom. How does the Báb speak of His prisons? What links His longing for sacrifice to the accounts of His martyrdom?

These readings stay in Ṭihrán. Bahá’u’lláh recalls being hurried along by a troop of executioners while a man on horseback snatched off His hat, four months in a place foul beyond comparison, feet in stocks and the most galling of chains, companions who were mostly thieves and highwaymen, two days without food, thumbs bound behind the back and an executioner who brought Him tea. Accounts by ‘Abdu’l-Bahá and others add the walk bareheaded and barefoot from Níyávarán, the chain that bound Him to five other Bábís, an attempt to poison Him, and a son’s glimpse of his Father at the noon airing of the prisoners. One passage recalls nights when He kissed the chains for love of God. What do these first-hand details add to the summaries? How can the same dungeon be both darkness and the place where chains were kissed?

These readings enter the Most Great Prison. Bahá’u’lláh records the first night in the barracks without food or drink, companions lying sick, three months without a bath, no barber admitted without guards, and seventy souls imprisoned with Him; twenty women entered the prison out of love. In one prayer He shows God His son blood-stained before Him. Reported talks describe the foul water and air, guards too sick to give water, a damp room with grass on its walls, thirteen people in one room, a carpet sold to bury two companions, and nine years without the sight of a green leaf. Yet the same readings speak of commemorating the Feast and the Riḍván Festival in the Prison and of joy beyond words in the direst straits. How do the readings hold these together? What is gained by naming this place the Most Great Prison?

These readings let Bahá’u’lláh speak of the weight of what befell Him. Twenty years, He tells the kings, have passed with the agony of a fresh tribulation each day; heaven, earth and mountains could not bear a single atom of it; were the sun acquainted with His sorrows it would rise no more. Reported talks take up why Christ prayed that the cup might pass, and note that Christ was opposed by the Jews while this Manifestation was opposed by the whole world. What pattern do these readings trace? How does knowing it change what a believer expects?

These readings give a purpose to the sufferings. Bahá’u’lláh writes that His body has borne imprisonment that the souls of others may be released from bondage and that He consented to be abased that they might be exalted; He chose imprisonment for Himself and freedom for His servants, and gives thanks for being imprisoned for the emancipation of the worlds. A prayer asks how, had He not been established in the Most Great Prison, the Cause could have spread abroad. Tribulation is called the oil for His Lamp and a help to this Revelation, and a reported talk says that under the chains He unfurled the flag of the oneness of humanity. Other passages say that those who imagine they can extinguish the light of God have grievously erred. What does it mean that one person’s suffering frees others? How is imprisonment turned into proclamation?

These readings speak of joy in tribulation. Bahá’u’lláh calls the pit His house and the prison His palace, anxiety His gladness and the prison His paradise, and says that the Youth has grown intimate with tribulations as infants with their mothers’ breasts. A prayer gives thanks that God has chosen the Prison as the throne of His kingdom; another exclaims how sweet is the injury suffered in His love; another wishes that life could be prolonged so as to be afflicted anew each day. Is this joy a denial of suffering or a way through it? Why might the homeland of those near to God be the prison?

These readings belong to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, a prisoner for forty years. He bids the friends rejoice in His bondage, which sows the seeds of freedom, calls the prison a palace and the cage a heavenly rose garden, and declines a release that notables could have procured because the citadel was the prison of the Abhá Beauty. He asks those who would pray for Him to pray that His tribulation be increased. Other passages show the cost: no one went to bed expecting to see the morrow, every loaf was cut open by the guard, enemies waited to cast Him into the sea or banish Him to Fezzan, and a prison was set within the prison. When the chains passed from His neck to ‘Abdu’l-Ḥamíd’s, He journeyed to the West. How did ‘Abdu’l-Bahá turn confinement into service? What does His refusal of release teach?

These readings turn to the believers. Bahá’u’lláh blesses those who have been imprisoned for His sake, tells a prisoner that He too is imprisoned by the decree of God, calls the humiliation of the loved ones the pride and glory of all temporal honour, and praises God for making the tyranny of the unjust a means whereby true lovers draw nigh. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that troubles come so that the friends may share in His tribulations, and rebukes tears over a few days of hardship borne in the footsteps of the Blessed Beauty. The readings recall believers who rushed dancing to the field of sacrifice and women paraded through the bazaars. One Tablet bids those who call themselves His lovers be ashamed of conduct unworthy of His sufferings, and prayers ask that hearts be made as strong as brass. How should a believer regard personal hardship in this light? What does it mean to share in another’s tribulation?

Compare the summaries of a life without a tranquil breath with the first-hand details of the dungeon in Ṭihrán, the house surrounded in Adrianople and the barracks of ‘Akká. What does each kind of account show that the other cannot?

How can a prison be called a palace, a paradise or a rose garden? Read the passages of the Báb, Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá that speak this way beside those describing foul air, hunger and chains. Is the change in the place, in the prisoner or in the purpose?

Bahá’u’lláh writes that His body bore imprisonment that the souls of others might be released from bondage. What kinds of freedom do the readings connect with His imprisonment, and how do they link suffering with the proclamation of the Cause from the prison?
Several passages say that His deepest grief came not from enemies but from those who claimed to love Him. Why might this be so, and what does it ask of those who call themselves His lovers?

What pattern do the readings trace in the opposition faced by Abraham, Moses, Christ, Muhammad, the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh? Who led the opposition in each case, and why do the readings say that it arose despite long expectation?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to share in His tribulations and to pray that His own be increased, while other prayers ask that the believers be kept steadfast and protected. How do the readings hold together the longing for tribulation and the prayer for relief and strength?
